title: Relational Algebra: Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Quick revision notes on the relational model (relations, keys, domains), the core algebra operators, joins and division, and how SQL maps onto algebra.

chapters.title: Relational Model and Keys
points: Relation = a set of tuples (rows) over a schema of attributes (columns); because it is a set, there are no duplicate tuples and row order is irrelevant
Domain = the set of allowed atomic values for an attribute (e.g. age: integers 0-150); degree = number of attributes, cardinality = number of tuples
Super key = any attribute set that uniquely identifies a tuple; candidate key = a minimal super key (drop any attribute and uniqueness is lost)
Primary key = the one candidate key chosen to identify tuples (no NULLs); alternate keys = the remaining candidate keys
Foreign key = attributes referencing a candidate/primary key of another (or the same) relation; its value must match an existing key value or be NULL (referential integrity)

chapters.title: Selection, Projection and Renaming
points: Selection σ_cond(R) keeps the rows satisfying a predicate; it preserves the schema and its result is never larger than R
Projection π_A,B(R) keeps only the listed columns and removes duplicate rows, so the result may have fewer tuples than R
Composition order matters: π_name(σ_age>20(R)) works, but σ_age>20(π_name(R)) fails because age was projected away
Selections commute: σ_c1(σ_c2(R)) = σ_c2(σ_c1(R)) = σ_c1∧c2(R)
Rename ρ_S(A→B)(R) changes relation or attribute names; it is required in self-joins and when a product has clashing attribute names

chapters.title: Set Operations and Cartesian Product
points: Union R ∪ S, intersection R ∩ S and difference R − S need union-compatible relations: same degree and matching attribute domains; result takes attribute names from R
Difference is not commutative (R − S ≠ S − R); intersection is derivable as R ∩ S = R − (R − S)
Cartesian product R × S pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S: degree = deg(R)+deg(S), cardinality = |R|·|S|
Product alone is rarely useful and produces meaningless pairs; follow it with a selection on matching keys to get a join
Typical 'not in' queries use difference: customers who never ordered = π_id(Customer) − π_cust_id(Order)

chapters.title: Joins and Division
points: Theta join R ⋈_θ S = σ_θ(R × S); equi-join is theta join with only = conditions; natural join ⋈ equates all same-named attributes and keeps one copy of each
Outer joins keep unmatched rows padded with NULL: left ⟕ keeps all of R, right ⟖ all of S, full ⟗ both; inner join drops unmatched tuples
Natural join pitfalls: with no common attributes it degenerates to a Cartesian product, and accidentally shared column names silently join on the wrong columns
Division R ÷ S returns values of the attributes in R but not in S that are paired with every tuple of S (the 'for all' query, e.g. students who took all required courses)
Division formula: R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R); result schema is attrs(R) − attrs(S)

chapters.title: How SQL Maps to Algebra
points: SELECT list = projection π, WHERE = selection σ, FROM with several tables = Cartesian product ×, JOIN ... ON = theta join ⋈_θ
Logical SQL order is FROM → WHERE → SELECT, mirroring π(σ(R × S)) in the algebra expression
UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT map to ∪ / ∩ / −; they remove duplicates by default, ALL keeps them
SQL tables are bags, not sets: SELECT keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is used, whereas algebra projection always removes them
Division has no SQL operator: write it with NOT EXISTS twice, or GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT x) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM S)

chapters.title: Relational Algebra Cheat Sheet
points: Operator table: σ select rows, π project columns, ρ rename, ∪ union, − difference, × product, ⋈ join, ÷ division
Fundamental (minimal) operators are σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ; intersection, joins and division are derived from them
Key hierarchy: super key ⊇ candidate key ⊇ primary key; foreign key points to a candidate/primary key
Union compatibility: same degree and same domains per column; join schema = union of attributes, product degree = sum
SQL map: SELECT→π, WHERE→σ, FROM a,b→×, JOIN→⋈, UNION/EXCEPT→∪/−, outer joins→⟕ ⟖ ⟗, division→NOT EXISTS twice or HAVING COUNT
